clue.text: Big English debt failure exposed to public ridicule

indicators.note: a failure is a breakdown, so the letters before it collapse and are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A huge English debt default leaves someone humiliated in public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failure' signals the anagram of BIG + E + DEBT. To gibbet someone was originally to hang them on a gallows for display, hence to hold them up to scorn.
explanation.definitionFit: To gibbet is figuratively to pillory or hold someone up to scorn, as a hanged body once was displayed.

clue.text: Immigrant involved in no crime

indicators.note: involved suggests tangled or entwined, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A newcomer to the country is caught up in no wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges NO CRIME.
explanation.definitionFit: An incomer is someone who has moved in from elsewhere, a synonym for a newcomer or immigrant.

clue.text: Money taken by carrier in American mid-West

indicators.note: the money is taken by the carrier, so it sits right before it in the answer

parts.note: bread is slang for money
a basket is something used to carry things

explanation.surface: Cash is collected by a delivery firm somewhere in the American Midwest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrier' reads as a courier firm but is a container used for carrying. The Breadbasket is the nickname of the US grain-growing Midwest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Breadbasket is a nickname for the grain-producing states of the American Midwest.

clue.text: Turn to tobacco

definitions.meaning: ... is tobacco sold as a ... roll

explanation.surface: Someone takes up smoking.
explanation.definitionFit: A twist is both a turning movement and a rope-like roll of chewing or pipe tobacco.

clue.text: Dick unconscious on watch

parts.note: dead to the world means fast asleep, so dead stands for unconscious
to eye something is to watch it

explanation.surface: A man named Dick is out cold while supposed to be on guard duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dick' is not a man's name here but half of Deadeye Dick, a nickname for a crack shot, so the clue defines by completing the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadeye Dick is the stock nickname for an expert marksman, so the word pairs with Dick.

clue.text: Business premises no longer freezing

parts.note: off means no longer happening or cancelled
ice is frozen water, so freezing suggests ice

explanation.surface: A firm's premises have finally had the heating fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'no longer freezing' as OFF ICE: a thing taken off the ice is no longer frozen.
explanation.definitionFit: An office is the room or building where business is carried on.

clue.text: Stuffed a tree that's rotten into small furnace

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are put into the furnace word, so it is a container signal

parts.note: an oven is a small enclosed furnace for heating or baking

indicators.note: something rotten has gone bad and falls apart, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A decayed tree is stuffed into a little stove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's rotten' turns A TREE into EATER, which goes 'into' OVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has overeaten has gorged themselves, the sense of being stuffed after a meal.

clue.text: Safari covering miles

indicators.note: the word Safari covers or contains the short run of letters inside it

explanation.surface: A safari trip spans many miles of ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covering' says Safari holds the answer inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Miles used informally means by a long way, as in miles better, which is the adverbial sense of far.

clue.text: The estate may be sheltered by this

definitions.text: The estate may be sheltered by this

parts.words: The estate may be sheltered by this
parts.note: the estate sounds like land or property, but here it is an estate car, a vehicle parked under a roofed shelter beside a house

explanation.surface: Some structure protects a whole landed estate.
explanation.walkthrough: An estate car is the British name for a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: A carport is an open-sided roofed shelter for parking a vehicle such as an estate car.

clue.text: Churchman gets a line wrong — a faulty type?

parts.note: a cleric is a member of the clergy
an error is a wrong or mistake

explanation.surface: A priest muddles a sentence of the liturgy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a faulty type?' is a typing slip, the kind of mistake a clerk makes; the question mark marks the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerical error is a mistake in copying or typing, so it is a fault in the typing, a typo.

clue.text: In the middle of a badly illuminated back street

indicators.note: back tells us to read the dimly lit word backwards

parts.note: something dim is poorly lit

explanation.surface: Someone stands in the middle of a dark back alley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like part of 'back street' but reverses DIM to MID.
explanation.definitionFit: Amidst is a preposition meaning among or surrounded by, the same as in the middle of.

clue.text: One who has the will to deal with the remainder

definitions.text: One who has the will to deal with the remainder

parts.words: One who has the will to deal with the remainder
parts.note: it reads as someone determined to handle leftovers, but the will is a legal testament and the remainder is the residue of an estate

explanation.surface: A determined person tackles whatever is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: The person named in a will to administer the estate, settling debts and distributing the residue.

clue.text: In future, not an alternative for an unlucky person

indicators.note: an alternative version of the letters is another arrangement of them

explanation.surface: In the time ahead, there is no other option for someone with bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternative' rearranges FUTURE NOT AN; 'In' and 'for an' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: An unfortunate, used as a noun, is a luckless or wretched person.

clue.text: The Times is not for everyone any more

definitions.text: The Times is not for everyone any more

parts.words: The Times is not for everyone any more
parts.note: it reads as the paper losing its general appeal, but it means the paper is no longer printed on large pages, the format meant to be spread broadly

explanation.surface: The Times newspaper has lost its mass readership.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times moved from large-format pages to the smaller compact format in 2004; broad here means widely, as in broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadsheet is a newspaper printed on large pages, the format The Times used before going compact.

clue.text: Get worse code in old computer

parts.note: to slide is to decline or deteriorate
a rule is part of a code of conduct

explanation.surface: Things deteriorate when an antique computer is programmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'code' suggests programming, but it is a set of rules.
explanation.definitionFit: A slide rule is a mechanical calculating device used before electronic calculators, humorously an old computer.

clue.text: Obese eastern lot

parts.note: obese means very fat

explanation.surface: An overweight person from the East has their destiny described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lot' is not a quantity but one's lot in life.
explanation.definitionFit: One's lot is one's destiny or what life allots, a synonym for fate.

clue.text: Reassuring report from one running this

indicators.note: a report is a sound, so the reassuring phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: I'm OK is the reassuring thing a person says

explanation.surface: A jogger gives a comforting update on their progress.
explanation.walkthrough: I'M OK, spoken, sounds like the answer; the definition needs the idiom run amok, so one running this is someone rampaging.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is to rampage wildly, so this word is what one runs when out of control.

clue.text: Some legionaries the steward caught out

indicators.note: out tells us the abbreviation for caught is removed from the steward

parts.note: a manciple is a steward who buys provisions for a college or inn, as in Chaucer
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Some Roman soldiers report that the household steward was caught away from his post.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaucer's Manciple in The Canterbury Tales is the famous steward.
explanation.definitionFit: A maniple was a subdivision of a Roman legion, a company of around 120 to 200 soldiers.

clue.text: Fierily destroy urge to accept New Age

indicators.note: the urging word takes in the other letters, so it is a container signal

parts.note: to incite is to urge or spur on
an era is an age or period

explanation.surface: Someone is pressed to embrace New Age beliefs and burn everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Age' looks like the spiritual movement, but it is two separate pieces; 'to accept' marks the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To incinerate is to burn something completely to ashes.

clue.text: Keeper's dog is over a hill

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
a tor is a rocky hill, common in Dartmoor place names

explanation.surface: A gamekeeper's dog has run over the brow of a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeper's' is Keeper is; in a down clue 'over' just places the dog above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A curator is the keeper of a museum or collection.

clue.text: I've gone off having an object in travel

indicators.note: gone off says the letters of I've have left the grammar word

parts.note: in grammar a transitive verb is one that takes a direct object

explanation.surface: Someone abandons a holiday because they object to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Transit is the act of travelling or being conveyed from place to place.

clue.text: Odd kit we ran in —- sweaters, for example

indicators.note: odd means strange or irregular, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A team runs out in peculiar strip made of jumpers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' rearranges KIT WE RAN; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Knitwear covers knitted garments, and sweaters are a typical example.

clue.text: Savage, but extremely honest

explanation.surface: A ferocious person turns out to be utterly candid.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense comes from phrases like brutal honesty: frankness with no softening.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutal means both cruelly violent and, of truth or honesty, harshly frank without softening.

clue.text: Fictitious university among the fens

indicators.note: the university letter sits among the marsh letters, so it is a container signal

parts.note: bogs are wet marshy ground like fens

explanation.surface: A made-up university is supposedly set in the Fens.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are marshland in eastern England, home to Cambridge, which gives the surface its sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Bogus means fake or sham, and so not genuine, like something fictitious.

clue.text: Annoy informer about to retire

indicators.note: about places the word to next to the informer word, ahead of it

parts.note: to put out someone is to annoy or inconvenience them
a grass is British slang for a police informer

explanation.surface: An irritated snitch is on the point of stepping down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as on the point of, but TO is a piece of its own. A grass is British slang for someone who informs to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: To put out to grass is to retire, as an old horse is sent off to pasture.

clue.text: Child's finger

definitions.meaning: a finger of spirits is a small measure, a dram

explanation.surface: A little one's finger.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as the clue's link (Child is finger) rather than a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A tot is both a small child and a small measure of spirits, the same quantity as a finger of whisky.

clue.text: The spirit of Britannia, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken and we hear a different spelling

parts.note: Britannia metal is a pewter-like alloy of tin, antimony and copper

explanation.surface: Britannia personifies the courage of the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Britannia, the figure of Britain, misleads; Britannia metal is an alloy, and METAL said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mettle means courage and strength of character, the spirit someone shows.

clue.text: They may be paid to relations

definitions.text: They may be paid to relations

parts.words: They may be paid to relations
parts.note: it suggests money handed to family members

explanation.surface: Family members receive some sort of payment.
explanation.definitionFit: One pays one's respects to someone, including relatives, as a courteous visit or show of regard.
